*Pre-Assignment*
Load all necessary packages, read in the clinical data.csv file you have in your analysis_data folder, and instantiate the MAF_object.
```{r}
library(maftools)

# read the clinical data created in the previous hw
clinic <- read.csv("/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/brca_clinical_data.csv")

# find the downloaded MAF file
maf_files <- list.files(
  "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/GDCdata",
  pattern = "\\.maf(\\.gz)?$",
  recursive = TRUE,
  full.names = TRUE
)

head(maf_files)
#instantiate MAF_object
maf_file <- maf_files[1]
MAF_object <- read.maf( maf = maf_file, clinicalData = clinic, isTCGA = TRUE)

#create figure directory to save images to
fig_dir <- "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/qbio_490_jennifer_jain/week6_genomics/figures"

dir.create(fig_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
```

It's useful to save your MAF_object, so that you don't have to go through the trouble of querying and preparing it everytime. The saveRDS function allows us to save an R object, allowing us to access it directly from our files. 
```{r}

saveRDS(MAF_object, file = "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds")
```

When you reopen a new R session and want to access your MAF_object, you can use the readRDS function to load the object back into a new variable.
```{r}
MAF_object <- readRDS(file = "/path/to/analysis_data/maf_object.rds")
# ex. MAF_object <- readRDS(file = "/home1/yourname/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds")
```

*1*
Choose a clinical variable (or any variable from clin_rad or clin_drug) to separate your populations into two different groups and rewrite the column or create a new column with that variable as a factor. ***Do not use age or vital_status as your clinical variable.*** Hint: if your variable is continuous, you will need to determine your own cutoffs for the different levels of the factor. If your variable is categorical and has more than two possible values, choose the two that are the most common.
```{r}
# I chose histological type as my clinical variable and compared
# infiltrating ductal carcinoma with infiltrating lobular carcinoma.
# these are the two most common histological groups in the dataset.
# I then converted these groups into a factor with two levels (ductal and lobular) using nested ifelse
clinic$histology_group <- ifelse(
  grepl("ductal", clinic$histological_type, ignore.case = TRUE), "Ductal",
  ifelse(
    grepl("lobular", clinic$histological_type, ignore.case = TRUE), "Lobular", NA))

clinic$histology_group <- factor(
  clinic$histology_group,
  levels = c("Ductal", "Lobular")
)

table(clinic$histology_group, useNA = "ifany")
```


*2*
Create a co-oncoplot with the top 10-20 (you choose) most mutated genes for the two groups. Pick one that has a large discrepancy in % mutated or type of mutations between the groups and research it. 
Research it. What is the gene used for? Can you think of any reason for the discrepancy?
```{r}
ductal_samples <- clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[
  clinic$histology_group == "Ductal" &
  !is.na(clinic$histology_group)
]

lobular_samples <- clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[
  clinic$histology_group == "Lobular" &
  !is.na(clinic$histology_group)
]

ductal_maf <- subsetMaf(
  maf = MAF_object,
  tsb = ductal_samples
)

lobular_maf <- subsetMaf(
  maf = MAF_object,
  tsb = lobular_samples
)

two_group_samples <- c(ductal_samples, lobular_samples)

two_group_maf <- subsetMaf(
  maf = MAF_object,
  tsb = two_group_samples
)

gene_summary <- getGeneSummary(two_group_maf)

top15_genes <- head(
  gene_summary$Hugo_Symbol,
  15
)

top15_genes

png(
  file.path(fig_dir, "01_co_oncoplot_ductal_vs_lobular_top15.png"),
  width = 2200,
  height = 1400,
  res = 180
)

coOncoplot(
  m1 = ductal_maf,
  m2 = lobular_maf,
  genes = top15_genes,
  m1Name = "Ductal",
  m2Name = "Lobular",
  removeNonMutated = TRUE
)

dev.off()
```
